rounds.t: Right-to-left shunts: the 5 T's and Ebstein anomaly

q.s: A newborn becomes deeply cyanotic within hours of birth. Which feature is typical of right-to-left shunt lesions?
o: Early cyanosis, often needing urgent surgery and/or prostaglandins to keep the PDA open
They are always asymptomatic at birth
They are treated with indomethacin to close the PDA
e: Correct. Right-to-left shunts cause early cyanosis ("blue babies").
Many depend on an open PDA.
That describes left-to-right shunts with Eisenmenger syndrome.

q.s: Which list correctly gives the 5 T's of right-to-left shunts?
o: Truncus, Tricuspid regurgitation, Tetralogy, Takayasu, TAPVR
Transposition, Tricuspid atresia, Tetralogy, Thoracic aneurysm, TAPVR
Truncus arteriosus, Transposition, Tricuspid atresia, Tetralogy of Fallot, TAPVR
Truncus, Transposition, Tricuspid atresia, Tetralogy of Fallot, Turner syndrome
e: Turner is a syndrome, not a shunt.

q.s: A cyanotic infant has a single great vessel arising from the heart. Which additional defect is present in most such patients?
e: Correct. Most patients with persistent truncus arteriosus have an accompanying VSD.

q.s: In D-transposition of the great arteries, which arrangement is present?
o: Aorta from RV (anterior), pulmonary trunk from LV (posterior)
Pulmonary veins draining to the RA
A single vessel from both ventricles
Aorta from LV, pulmonary trunk from RV
e: Correct. This separates the systemic and pulmonary circulations.

q.s: A newborn with D-transposition survives the first days of life. What must be present?
o: A shunt allowing mixing, such as a VSD, PDA, or patent foramen ovale
e: Correct. TGA is incompatible with life without mixing.

q.s: A chest x-ray of a cyanotic newborn shows an "egg on a string" appearance. Which embryologic failure caused this?
o: Anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum
Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to form at all
Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral
e: Correct. This produces D-TGA with a narrow superior mediastinum.

q.s: Without surgical correction, what is the typical outcome of D-transposition of the great arteries?
o: Most infants die within the first few months of life
Progression to Eisenmenger syndrome in adulthood
e: Infants rarely survive that long untreated.

q.s: An infant with absence of the tricuspid valve and a hypoplastic RV is cyanotic. Which ECG findings are expected?
o: Pseudo-RBBB with ST elevation in V1–V3
RA hypertrophy (tall P waves) and LV hypertrophy (left axis deviation)

q.s: For viability, tricuspid atresia requires which defects?
o: Both an ASD and a VSD or PDA
e: An ASD is needed to leave the RA.
Blood must reach the left heart first, through an ASD.

q.s: Tetralogy of Fallot is caused by:
o: Downward displacement of the tricuspid valve
Failure of neural crest cells to form the truncal ridges
Anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum
Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral

q.s: The four components of tetralogy of Fallot are remembered as PROVe. Which component is the most important determinant of prognosis?
e: Not one of the four components.

q.s: A 3-year-old with a cyanotic heart defect squats after running and his cyanosis improves. How does squatting help?
A child's chest x-ray shows a "boot-shaped" heart. Which component of the child's lesion produces this shape?
e: Gives the "egg on a string" of TGA.
Not the cause of the boot shape.
Correct. RVH in tetralogy of Fallot gives a boot-shaped heart.

q.s: A child with tetralogy of Fallot has episodes of severe cyanosis when crying or febrile. These "tet spells" result from:
o: Exacerbation of RV outflow obstruction, ↑ right-to-left flow across the VSD

q.s: Tetralogy of Fallot is most strongly associated with which genetic syndrome?
e: Associated with coarctation and bicuspid valve.
Associated with MVP and aortic aneurysm.

q.s: Which is the most common cause of early childhood cyanosis?
e: Correct. TOF is the most common cause of early childhood cyanosis.
TGA presents with cyanosis in the neonatal period; FA names TOF as the most common cause of early childhood cyanosis.

q.s: In total anomalous pulmonary venous return, the pulmonary veins drain into the right heart circulation. What additional defect maintains cardiac output?
o: An ASD, sometimes with a PDA, allowing right-to-left shunting

q.s: A newborn whose mother took a mood stabilizer during pregnancy has tricuspid leaflets displaced into the RV, "atrializing" part of the ventricle. Which drug was most likely taken?
e: Correct. In utero lithium exposure is linked to Ebstein anomaly.

q.s: Ebstein anomaly is associated with which findings?
o: Tricuspid regurgitation, accessory conduction pathways, and right-sided HF

q.s: Which right-to-left shunt has "3" in its mnemonic count, reflecting "Tri"?

rounds.t: Left-to-right shunts, Eisenmenger, coarctation, and associations

q.s: What is the order of frequency of left-to-right shunts?
Cardiac catheterization in a child shows ↑ O2 saturation in the RV and pulmonary artery but not in the RA. Which defect is most likely?
e: PDA raises saturation in the pulmonary artery only.
A right-to-left shunt lowers systemic saturation.
ASD raises saturation in the RA too.
Correct. VSD ↑ O2 saturation in the RV and pulmonary artery.

q.s: Catheterization shows a step-up in O2 saturation in the RA, RV, and pulmonary artery. Which defect is present?
e: Step-up is in the pulmonary artery.

q.s: What is the most common type of ASD?
e: PFO is distinct, a failed fusion rather than a true septal defect.

q.s: How does a patent foramen ovale differ from an atrial septal defect?
o: PFO is associated with Down syndrome
PFO is due to failed fusion of the septa, whereas ASD is a true defect in the interatrial septum
PFO is a larger tissue deficit

q.s: A man with an ASD has a stroke while lifting weights. What explains the embolus?
o: Temporary shunt reversal lets venous emboli cross the ASD into the systemic circulation
Infective endocarditis of the mitral valve

q.s: In the neonatal period, why does PDA shunt direction change from right-to-left to left-to-right?
o: Closure of the foramen ovale reverses all flow

q.s: Patency of the ductus arteriosus is maintained by:
o: PGE synthesis and low O2 tension
High O2 tension and low PGE

q.s: An adult with an uncorrected PDA has cyanosis and clubbing of the toes but pink fingers. This is called:
o: Differential cyanosis from late shunt reversal
e: Correct. Deoxygenated blood enters the aorta distal to the arm vessels.

q.s: A 30-year-old with an uncorrected VSD develops cyanosis, clubbing, and polycythemia. Why did the shunt reverse?
o: ↑ pulmonary flow → pulmonary vascular remodeling → pulmonary arterial hypertension → RVH until RV pressure > LV pressure
LV pressure rose above RV pressure

q.s: Which findings are typical of Eisenmenger syndrome?
o: Wide pulse pressure and bounding pulses
e: Seen in AR or PDA without reversal.

q.s: A 16-year-old girl with short stature and a webbed neck has hypertension in her arms and weak, delayed femoral pulses. Which lesion is most likely?
e: Can cause pulse deficits but the syndrome points to coarctation.
Correct. Associated with Turner syndrome and brachiofemoral delay.

q.s: In an adult with long-standing coarctation, a chest x-ray shows notching of the inferior rib margins. What causes this?
o: Enlarged intercostal arteries forming collateral circulation

q.s: Coarctation of the aorta is associated with which vascular complication in the brain?
e: Linked to hypertension generally, not the listed complication.

q.s: A newborn born through meconium-stained amniotic fluid has tachypnea, cyanosis with preductal O2 saturation higher than postductal, and equal pulses. What is the diagnosis?
o: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
e: Doesn't cause differential pre/postductal saturation this way.
Correct. Persistent ↑ PVR drives right-to-left shunting through the foramen ovale and ductus.
q.k: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn

q.s: An infant of a mother with poorly controlled diabetes during pregnancy is most at risk for which cardiac defect?
e: Correct. Also truncus arteriosus, tricuspid atresia, and VSD.

q.s: A child with "elfin" facies, hypercalcemia, and a very friendly personality has which cardiac lesion?
A newborn with congenital rubella syndrome (cataracts, deafness) most likely has which cardiac defects?
o: PDA, pulmonary artery stenosis, and septal defects

q.s: A newborn with Down syndrome is screened by echocardiography. Which defects are most associated with this syndrome?
A child with a smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, and growth restriction after heavy prenatal alcohol exposure is most at risk for which cardiac defects?
o: VSD, PDA, ASD, and tetralogy of Fallot

q.s: Hypertension is defined as persistent BP of:
e: The current FA threshold is lower.

q.s: What proportion of hypertension is primary (essential)?
e: Correct. Related to ↑ CO or ↑ TPR.

q.s: A 32-year-old woman has resistant hypertension and an abdominal bruit. Renal angiography shows a "string of beads" appearance of the renal artery. Diagnosis?
e: Affects the aorta and branches with pulse loss.
Correct. Usually seen in adult females.
Microaneurysms, not string of beads in this context.

q.s: A patient has BP 195/125 mm Hg with no headache, chest pain, neurologic deficit, or lab abnormality. This is:
e: Correct. Severe hypertension (≥ 180/≥ 120) without acute end-organ damage.

q.s: A patient with BP 210/130 mm Hg has papilledema and confusion. Which arteriolar change may be seen?
e: Seen in chronic benign hypertension and diabetes.

q.s: Concentric LVH in hypertension is mediated by which factors?
A 40-year-old man with familial hypercholesterolemia has firm nodules on his Achilles tendons. These are:
A 35-year-old has a white-gray ring at the edge of his cornea. Why is this significant?
o: It is always normal at any age
Corneal arcus at a young age suggests hypercholesterolemia
e: Common in older adults but earlier onset suggests hypercholesterolemia.

q.s: Atherosclerosis involves deposition of lipid plaque in which layer of the arterial wall?
e: Medial disease includes cystic medial degeneration and Monckeberg calcification.

q.s: Which ranks the sites of atherosclerosis from most to least commonly involved?
o: Coronary > abdominal aorta > carotid > popliteal > circle of Willis
Abdominal aorta > coronary > popliteal > carotid > circle of Willis
Carotid > coronary > abdominal aorta > popliteal > circle of Willis
Circle of Willis > carotid > coronary > popliteal > abdominal aorta
Popliteal > abdominal aorta > coronary > carotid > circle of Willis

q.s: Which is a non-modifiable risk factor for atherosclerosis?
e: Correct. Age, male sex, postmenopausal status, and family history are non-modifiable.

q.s: In atherosclerotic plaque progression, smooth muscle cell migration into the intima is driven by:
Which sequence best describes atherosclerosis progression?
o: Fatty streak → endothelial dysfunction → foam cells → fibrous plaque
Endothelial dysfunction → macrophage/LDL accumulation → foam cells → fatty streak → SMC migration → fibrous plaque → complex atheroma → calcification
Calcification → fatty streak → fibrous plaque → foam cells
SMC migration → endothelial dysfunction → foam cells → fatty streak

q.s: How do statins reduce cardiovascular events in atherosclerosis?
o: They ↓ LDL, ↓ plaque progression, and ↓ risk of plaque rupture

q.s: In atherosclerotic plaque, what does calcium content correlate with?
Two days after cardiac catheterization, a 68-year-old man has livedo reticularis, painful blue toes with palpable pedal pulses, and rising creatinine. Diagnosis?
e: Correct. Microemboli from aortic plaque; large arteries stay patent.

q.s: A patient with long-standing diabetes has renal arterioles with homogeneous pink wall thickening. Which process is responsible?
o: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis from plasma protein leak into the subendothelium

q.s: A biopsy from a patient with malignant hypertension shows concentric "onion skin" thickening of arterioles. This represents:
o: Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis with smooth muscle proliferation

q.s: Which complication is NOT typically listed as a consequence of atherosclerosis?
e: Correct. That results from rheumatic fever, not atherosclerosis.

q.s: Long-standing hypertension predisposes to which group of conditions?
o: Aortic stenosis, mitral prolapse, and myxoma
CAD, concentric LVH, HF, atrial fibrillation, aortic dissection, stroke, CKD, and retinopathy

rounds.t: Aortic disease, subclavian steal, and angina

q.s: A 70-year-old smoker has a pulsatile periumbilical mass. Which statement about his condition is correct?
o: It most often occurs above the renal arteries
It is most common in women
It is associated with cystic medial degeneration
It involves transmural inflammation and ECM degradation; smoking is the strongest risk factor
e: Male sex is a risk factor.

q.s: Why are abdominal aortic aneurysms most often infrarenal?
o: The distribution of vasa vasorum is reduced there

q.s: A man presents with sudden abdominal and back pain, a pulsatile abdominal mass, and hypotension resistant to fluids. Diagnosis?
e: Possible but the triad indicates AAA rupture.

q.s: A 28-year-old tall man with long fingers has a dilated aortic root and a diastolic murmur. Which pathologic process underlies his aortic disease?
e: Correct. Thoracic aortic aneurysm associated with Marfan syndrome.

q.s: Tertiary syphilis causes thoracic aortic aneurysm through:
o: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum

q.s: After a high-speed car crash, a patient has a widened mediastinum on x-ray. Where is traumatic aortic rupture most likely?
o: Ascending aorta at the sinotubular junction
Aortic isthmus, just distal to the left subclavian artery origin

q.s: A 60-year-old with poorly controlled hypertension has sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the back and a 30 mm Hg BP difference between arms. What is the strongest risk factor for this condition?
e: A risk factor but not the strongest overall.
A risk factor but not the strongest.
Correct. Hypertension is the strongest risk factor for aortic dissection.

q.s: A Stanford type A aortic dissection involves the ascending aorta. Which complication can occur and what is the treatment?
o: Acute aortic regurgitation or cardiac tamponade; surgery

q.s: A Stanford type B aortic dissection involves only the descending aorta. How is it initially treated?
A 65-year-old has dizziness and left arm pain when using his left arm. His left arm systolic BP is 25 mm Hg lower than the right. What is happening in the left vertebral artery?
o: Reversed flow, stealing blood from the brain to supply the arm

q.s: What is the most common cause of subclavian steal syndrome?
e: Correct. Takayasu arteritis and heart surgery are other causes.
A cause but not the most common.

q.s: Stable angina is usually due to atherosclerosis with what degree of coronary occlusion?
e: Too little to cause angina typically.

q.s: A 58-year-old man has chest pain at rest that has increased in frequency over 2 days. Troponin is normal. ECG shows ST depression. Diagnosis?
e: Correct. Thrombosis with incomplete occlusion; no biomarker elevation.
Stable angina is exertional and predictable.
Transient ST elevation, often in smokers.

q.s: A 40-year-old smoker has early-morning chest pain at rest with transient ST elevations that resolve. Which triggers are associated with this condition?
Which treatment is appropriate for vasospastic (Prinzmetal) angina?
o: Ca2+ channel blockers, nitrates, and smoking cessation

q.s: An elderly woman with stable angina develops pneumonia with sustained tachycardia and hypotension; troponin rises but angiography shows no plaque rupture. What caused the MI?
Which pattern distinguishes NSTEMI from STEMI?
o: NSTEMI is a subendocardial infarct with ST depression/T inversion; STEMI is transmural with ST elevation and pathologic Q waves

q.s: Which is a recognized risk factor for thoracic aortic aneurysm?
o: Tobacco smoking as the strongest factor
Hypertension, bicuspid aortic valve, or connective tissue disease such as Marfan syndrome

q.s: A patient with a known aortic aneurysm develops new abdominal and back pain. What does this pain signal?
o: Renal colic unrelated to the aneurysm
e: New pain is a warning sign.

q.s: A patient with suspected aortic dissection has a chest x-ray. Which finding is expected?

rounds.t: Ischemic heart disease, MI evolution, and diagnosis

q.s: During a dipyridamole stress test, a patient with a severe coronary stenosis develops ischemia. What mechanism explains this?
o: Coronary steal: dilating normal vessels shunts blood away from maximally dilated vessels beyond the stenosis

q.s: Sudden cardiac death is most commonly due to:
o: A lethal ventricular arrhythmia such as ventricular fibrillation

q.s: Coronary artery disease accounts for approximately what proportion of sudden cardiac deaths?
How is sudden cardiac death prevented in high-risk patients?
A patient with stable angina has LV systolic dysfunction that improves after revascularization. This phenomenon is:
e: Correct. Chronic ischemia causes reversible dysfunction.
Stunning follows brief acute ischemia and is transient.

q.s: After a brief episode of acute ischemia that is promptly reperfused, LV systolic function is transiently reduced and then recovers. This is called:
Which coronary arteries are most commonly occluded in MI, in order?
A man dies 2 hours after MI onset. What would light microscopy of the infarcted myocardium most likely show?
e: Correct. Wavy fibers appear at 0–4 hours.

q.s: A patient with an acute MI receives a stent and reperfusion. Biopsy shows dark eosinophilic bands in myocytes. What causes this change?
o: Reperfusion injury: free radicals and ↑ Ca2+ influx → hypercontraction of myofibrils

q.s: Three days after MI, a patient develops pleuritic chest pain and a friction rub. Histology of the infarct at this time would show:
o: Extensive coagulative necrosis with neutrophils at the margins

q.s: Seven days after MI, a patient suddenly develops hypotension and JVD and dies. Why is the myocardium most vulnerable to rupture at this time?
o: Dense scar is stiff and brittle
Macrophage-mediated degradation with early granulation tissue weakens the wall

q.s: At autopsy 2 months after an MI, the infarct site is a contracted gray-white scar. Which complication is associated with this phase?
o: True ventricular aneurysm with risk of mural thrombus

q.s: On tetrazolium staining of a heart with a recent infarct, how does infarcting tissue appear?
e: Correct. Healthy tissue stains dark; infarcting tissue stains pale.

q.s: In the first 6 hours of a suspected MI, the gold standard for diagnosis is:
Cardiac troponin I rises about 4 hours after MI. When does it peak and how long does it stay elevated?
o: Peaks at 1 hour; normal by 6 hours
Peaks at 24 hours; stays elevated 7–10 days
Peaks at 1 week; stays elevated 1 month
Peaks at 6 hours; normal by 24 hours
Peaks at 3 days; normal by day 4

q.s: A patient has recurrent chest pain 4 days after an MI. Historically, which marker was used to detect reinfarction because it normalizes within 2–3 days?
e: Correct. It's now largely replaced by high-sensitivity troponin.

q.s: An ECG shows ST elevations in leads II, III, and aVF. Which infarct location and artery are most likely?
e: V7–V9 with ST depression in V1–V3.

q.s: An ECG shows ST elevations in V1–V2. Which infarct location is indicated?
An ECG shows ST depression in V1–V3 with tall R waves. Which infarct is suggested?
e: ST elevation would be in V1–V2.
Correct. Confirmed by ST elevation in V7–V9.

q.s: ST elevations in leads I and aVL indicate infarction of which region and artery?
A 72-year-old with hypertension has an irregularly irregular pulse. ECG shows no discrete P waves and an irregular baseline. Where does the arrhythmogenic activity usually originate?
o: Automatic foci near the pulmonary vein ostia in the left atrium

q.s: In atrial fibrillation, which is the most common site of thrombus formation?
The ABCD mnemonic for atrial fibrillation management stands for:
o: Anticoagulation, Beta-blockers, Calcium channel blockers, Digoxin

q.s: A patient with a severe COPD exacerbation has an irregularly irregular rhythm with at least 3 distinct P wave morphologies. Diagnosis?
e: Correct. Multiple ectopic atrial foci, associated with COPD, pneumonia, HF.

q.s: An ECG shows regular "sawtooth" atrial waves with a 4:1 conduction ratio. Where does this arrhythmia usually originate?
o: A reentry circuit around the tricuspid annulus

q.s: Atrial flutter can be definitively treated by catheter ablation of which region?
o: The region between the tricuspid annulus and the IVC

q.s: A 25-year-old woman has sudden-onset palpitations and lightheadedness. ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 180/min. What is the first step to terminate it?
e: Correct. PSVT is terminated by slowing AV nodal conduction.

q.s: PSVT is most often due to a reentrant tract located:
o: Between atrium and ventricle, most commonly in the AV node

q.s: A young man's ECG shows a short PR interval, a slurred upstroke of the QRS, and a widened QRS. Which structure causes this?
o: Bundle of Kent bypassing the AV node
Accessory pathway around the tricuspid annulus causing flutter
e: Correct. Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome with a delta wave.

q.s: A patient with WPW develops a rapid tachycardia. Which drug should be avoided?
e: Correct. AV nodal blockers (adenosine, CCBs, β-blockers) can favor conduction down the accessory pathway.

q.s: A narrow-complex tachycardia has QRS duration below what value?
e: Below normal QRS but not the cutoff used.

q.s: A 60-year-old with a prior large MI has a regular wide-complex tachycardia at 170/min. What is the most likely cause and risk?
o: Ventricular tachycardia from post-MI scar; high risk of sudden cardiac death
e: Flutter is narrow complex unless aberrant.

q.s: A patient on methadone and ondansetron develops a polymorphic VT with shifting sinusoidal waveforms. ECG before the event showed a long QT. She is hemodynamically stable. Treatment?
Which electrolyte abnormalities predispose to torsades de pointes?
The ABCDEF+NO mnemonic lists drugs that prolong QT. Which group is included?
o: Antibiotics such as macrolides and fluoroquinolones

q.s: Which antifungal is listed among drugs causing QT prolongation?
A man collapses; the monitor shows a disorganized rhythm with no identifiable waves. What is required?
e: VF has no QRS to synchronize.
Correct. Ventricular fibrillation is fatal without them.

q.s: A 35-year-old Asian man with a family history of sudden death has a pseudo-RBBB pattern with ST elevation in V1–V3. What is the most common genetic cause?
o: Loss-of-function Na+ channel mutation, autosomal dominant
e: Correct. Brugada syndrome; prevent SCD with ICD.

q.s: A child with congenital sensorineural deafness has a long QT interval. Which syndrome and inheritance pattern?
o: Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome; autosomal recessive

q.s: An 80-year-old has bradycardia, sinus pauses, and junctional escape beats due to age-related SA node degeneration. Diagnosis?

rounds.t: Conduction blocks, premature beats, MI complications, ACS treatment

q.s: An asymptomatic man has a constant PR interval of 240 msec with every P followed by a QRS. Management?
o: None required; first-degree AV block is benign

q.s: ECG shows progressive PR lengthening until a P wave is not followed by a QRS, with a regularly irregular pattern. Diagnosis?
e: PR doesn't change before dropped beats.
Correct. Usually asymptomatic; no treatment required.

q.s: Why does Mobitz type II block usually require a pacemaker?
o: It is caused by digoxin toxicity
It may progress to third-degree block, as it usually indicates a structural abnormality such as ischemia or fibrosis

q.s: A hiker from New England has fatigue, a past expanding rash, and an ECG showing P waves and QRS complexes beating independently with atrial rate > ventricular rate. Which infection can cause this block?
e: Causes myocarditis but not the classic listed cause.
Correct. Lyme disease can cause third-degree AV block.

q.s: What is the treatment of third-degree (complete) AV block?
In left bundle branch block, how does the left ventricle depolarize?
o: Via slower myocyte-to-myocyte conduction from the right ventricle
Through the left bundle at normal speed

q.s: A man who drinks lots of coffee has occasional extra beats; ECG shows a narrow QRS preceded by an early P wave. What is this and what risk does it carry?
o: Premature atrial contraction; benign but may ↑ risk of atrial fibrillation and flutter
Mobitz II; progression to complete block
PVC; high risk of sudden death
Junctional escape beat; complete heart block

q.s: A premature ventricular contraction on ECG appears as:
o: Narrow QRS with a preceding P wave
Dropped QRS after a P wave
Wide QRS with no preceding P wave
e: Correct. SV is ↓ due to shortened filling time.

q.s: What is an important cause of death before reaching the hospital and within the first 48 hours after MI?
Two days after MI, a patient has pleuritic chest pain and a friction rub. Diagnosis and prognosis?
Five days after an inferior MI, a patient develops acute pulmonary edema and a new holosystolic apical murmur. Why is the posteromedial papillary muscle more vulnerable than the anterolateral?
o: It is supplied by the LAD only
It has a single blood supply (PDA), whereas the anterolateral has dual supply (LAD and LCX)

q.s: Four days after MI, a patient develops cardiogenic shock and a new harsh holosystolic murmur. Catheterization shows ↑ O2 saturation and ↑ pressure in the RV. Diagnosis?
e: Correct. Macrophage-mediated degradation creates a VSD.
Causes MR without RV O2 step-up.

q.s: How does a ventricular pseudoaneurysm differ from a true ventricular aneurysm?
o: A true aneurysm forms at 3–14 days
A pseudoaneurysm contains all three wall layers
Both are equally likely to rupture
A pseudoaneurysm is a contained free wall rupture without endocardium or myocardium and is more likely to rupture
e: True aneurysms form weeks to months later.

q.s: Which factor is protective against ventricular free wall rupture after MI?
o: LV hypertrophy and prior post-MI scar tissue

q.s: Three months after MI, an outward bulge of the LV wall moves paradoxically with contraction (dyskinesia). Which complication is this?
e: Correct. Associated with fibrosis and mural thrombus.

q.s: Six weeks after MI, a patient has fever and pericarditis. What is the mechanism?
o: Autoimmune reaction: released cardiac antigens form immune complexes that deposit in the pericardium

q.s: For STEMI, which therapy is most important beyond anticoagulation, antiplatelets, β-blockers, ACE inhibitors, and statins?
o: Reperfusion, with PCI preferred over fibrinolysis

q.s: A patient with an inferior STEMI from RCA occlusion becomes hypotensive after nitroglycerin. What explains this and how should it be managed?
o: RV involvement makes CO preload-dependent; support preload with IV fluids and avoid nitroglycerin

q.s: In unstable angina/NSTEMI, which combination of antiplatelet therapy is used?
o: Aspirin plus an ADP receptor inhibitor such as clopidogrel

q.s: In the ECG of a premature ventricular contraction, why is stroke volume of that beat reduced?
What is the most common cardiomyopathy?
A 45-year-old with familial dilated cardiomyopathy has a mutation causing a shortened sarcomeric protein. Which gene is most likely involved?
e: Correct. "Titin is thin, myosin is more."

q.s: A patient with breast cancer treated with an anthracycline develops HF with a dilated LV. Which drug is responsible?
e: Associated with reversible cardiotoxicity but not the listed drug.

q.s: Which is a parasitic cause of dilated cardiomyopathy?
In dilated cardiomyopathy, sarcomeres are added:
Which findings are typical of dilated cardiomyopathy?
o: S4, systolic murmur that increases with Valsalva
HF, S3, systolic regurgitant murmur, and a balloon-shaped heart on CXR

q.s: A woman develops chest pain and transient LV apical ballooning after her husband's sudden death. Coronaries are normal. Mechanism?
A 17-year-old athlete collapses and dies during a game. Autopsy shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy with myofibrillar disarray. What is the inheritance and typical mutation?
o: Autosomal dominant; β-myosin heavy chain or myosin-binding protein C
e: DCM is often titin and familial dominant.

q.s: In hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy, what causes LV outflow obstruction?
o: Asymmetric septal hypertrophy with systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve

q.s: Which drugs should be avoided in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
o: Drugs that ↓ preload, such as diuretics and vasodilators

q.s: Which drug is used for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy refractory to β-blockers or nondihydropyridine CCBs?
The PLEASe Help! mnemonic lists causes of restrictive/infiltrative cardiomyopathy. Which is included?
e: Correct. Postradiation fibrosis, Löffler endocarditis, Endocardial fibroelastosis, Amyloidosis, Sarcoidosis, Hemochromatosis.

q.s: A 68-year-old with nephrotic syndrome and HF has a thick-walled LV on echo but low-voltage QRS on ECG. Diagnosis?
e: Correct. Low voltage despite thick myocardium.

q.s: A patient with hypereosinophilic syndrome develops restrictive cardiomyopathy. Biopsy shows eosinophilic myocardial infiltrates. Diagnosis?
In heart failure with reduced EF (systolic dysfunction), which change is expected?
o: ↑ EDV with ↓ contractility, often from ischemia or dilated cardiomyopathy

q.s: What is the most common cause of right heart failure?
e: Causes acute cor pulmonale but not most common.

q.s: Which drugs reduce mortality in HFrEF?
o: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, ARNIs, β-blockers, and aldosterone antagonists

q.s: A patient with HF wakes up breathless 2 hours after falling asleep. What explains this?
o: ↑ venous return from blood redistribution and reabsorption of peripheral edema

q.s: Lung tissue from a patient with chronic left HF shows hemosiderin-laden macrophages. What are these called?
A patient with right HF has a mottled liver at autopsy. What is this appearance called?

rounds.t: High-output HF, shock, tamponade, syncope, and endocarditis

q.s: High-output heart failure results from:
o: ↓ SVR from vasodilation or arteriovenous shunting

q.s: Which is a cause of high-output heart failure?
e: Correct. Also obesity, cirrhosis, anemia, hyperthyroidism, Paget disease.

q.s: A trauma patient has hemorrhage. Which hemodynamic profile is expected?
A patient with a massive anterior MI has cold, clammy skin and pulmonary edema. Which profile is expected?
A patient with a large saddle pulmonary embolism is in shock. What are CVP and PCWP?
e: Correct. Obstructive shock from PE or tension pneumothorax.

q.s: A patient in early septic shock has warm, dry skin. What profile is expected?
A patient with a cervical spinal cord injury is hypotensive and bradycardic with warm skin. Which profile fits?
o: ↓ CVP, ↓ PCWP, ↓ CO, ↓ SVR, normal or ↑ SvO2

q.s: A patient with a stab wound has hypotension, distended neck veins, and distant heart sounds. Which finding is characteristic?
o: Equalization of diastolic pressures in all four chambers
Unequal diastolic pressures in the chambers

q.s: An ECG in a patient with a large pericardial effusion shows beat-to-beat variation in QRS amplitude. What is this called and why?
o: Delta waves from an accessory pathway
Electrical alternans from the "swinging" heart in a large effusion

q.s: Which echocardiographic finding is seen in cardiac tamponade?
o: Systolic RA collapse, diastolic RV collapse, and IVC plethora
Diastolic RA collapse and systolic RV collapse

q.s: Pulsus paradoxus is defined as:
o: ↓ diastolic BP > 20 mm Hg on standing
↓ systolic BP > 10 mm Hg during inspiration
↑ systolic BP > 10 mm Hg on inspiration

q.s: The mnemonic "pea COAT" lists causes of pulsus paradoxus. Which is included?
e: Correct. Croup, OSA, Asthma, COPD, Tamponade, plus constrictive pericarditis.

q.s: Orthostatic hypotension is defined as a fall in BP within 3 minutes of standing of:
A young woman faints after standing for a long time in a hot room, with warmth, pallor, and nausea beforehand, and recovers quickly. Which syncope type?
A patient with injection drug use has fever and a new murmur. Which valve is characteristically involved?
e: Most common overall, but not the IDU association.

q.s: A patient with a prosthetic valve placed 1 year ago develops endocarditis. Which organism is classically associated?
A man with endocarditis due to Streptococcus gallolyticus (bovis) should be evaluated for:
A patient with endocarditis has painful, raised violaceous nodules on the finger pads. These are:
e: Painless, flat, on palms or soles; vascular phenomena.

q.s: Acute infective endocarditis on a previously normal valve with large destructive vegetations is classically caused by:
A patient has endocarditis with negative blood cultures. Which organisms are classically culture negative?
e: Grow in culture; associated with IDU.

rounds.t: Rheumatic fever, pericardial disease, myocarditis, and tumors

q.s: A 60-year-old with metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma has an embolic stroke. Echo shows small sterile vegetations on the mitral valve. Diagnosis?
e: Correct. Associated with the hypercoagulable state of malignancy.

q.s: Rheumatic fever follows pharyngeal infection with which organism?
What is the mechanism of rheumatic heart disease?
o: Type II hypersensitivity: antibodies to M protein cross-react with self antigens such as myosin (molecular mimicry)
Direct bacterial invasion of the valves

q.s: Which valves are affected by rheumatic heart disease, from most to least common?
e: Correct. High-pressure valves are affected most.

q.s: A child with recent pharyngitis has migratory polyarthritis, carditis, and an evanescent rash with ring margins. Which major criterion does the rash represent?
Myocardial biopsy in acute rheumatic carditis shows granulomas with giant cells and enlarged macrophages with wavy, rodlike nuclei. These macrophages are:
Which lab tests support a diagnosis of rheumatic fever?
o: ↑ anti-streptolysin O and ↑ anti-DNase B titers

q.s: An older man has an aortic root aneurysm with "tree bark" appearance of the aorta and aortic insufficiency. Which infection is responsible?
A young man has sharp chest pain that improves when sitting forward, a friction rub, and diffuse ST elevations with PR depression. First-line treatment?
A patient with ESRD develops pericarditis. What specific treatment is indicated?
In resource-limited countries, what is the most common cause of constrictive pericarditis?
e: Common elsewhere but not the listed answer.

q.s: A patient's JVP rises during inspiration instead of falling. This is Kussmaul sign. Which condition is associated?
e: Correct. Also restrictive cardiomyopathy, right HF, massive PE, and RA/RV tumors.

q.s: A 30-year-old has fever, chest pain, and tachycardia out of proportion to fever after a viral illness. Biopsy shows lymphocytic infiltrate with focal necrosis. Diagnosis?
e: Correct. A major cause of SCD in adults < 40.

q.s: A man with recurrent nosebleeds, tongue telangiectasias, GI bleeding, and a lung AVM has which disorder and inheritance?
What is the most common cardiac tumor overall?
e: Most common primary tumor in children.
Most common primary tumor in adults.

q.s: A 50-year-old woman has episodic syncope, fever, weight loss, and an early diastolic "tumor plop." Echo shows a pedunculated LA mass. Which cytokine produced by the tumor causes her constitutional symptoms?
An infant with tuberous sclerosis has a ventricular mass. What is it?
Where do most cardiac myxomas occur?
e: Correct. "Ball valve" LA obstruction can cause syncope.

q.s: Which is a bacterial cause of myocarditis?
e: Correct. Also Borrelia burgdorferi and Mycoplasma pneumoniae.

q.s: A patient with prior thoracic radiotherapy has dyspnea, edema, JVD, and an early diastolic sound after S2. Echo shows a thick pericardium limiting ventricular filling. What is the sound?
